name: London
narrative_excerpt: D: House sold! We went to the Morgans’ to stay the night. Car broke down twice, oh dear! We were late to have our last cholera injections.

name: Aachen
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We finally left England safely after some rather worrying problems with the sale of the house, and with Fred – this turned out to be the ignition coil.

name: Munich
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We drove to Munich to see our Estonian friends, the Nahas. We took the opportunity to take the children round the magnificent Science and Technology Museum.

name: Villach
narrative_excerpt: D: Found a place in a little forest to sleep – wet, but nice. In morning, made houses for Paddington Bear, and took thing out of my ear, can’t swim for 3/4 days. Drove into Salzburg to see old city, but couldn’t really find it.

name: Postojna
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We saw some fabulous caves at Postojna, just before reaching the Adriatic coast. An electric train took us 3 km underground before we started walking through gallery after gallery of stalagmites and stalactites, of various colours and shapes.

name: Omiš
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Stayed night at a very nice camp a few miles past Omis, in a pine forest going down to a stony beach.

name: Dubrovnik
narrative_excerpt: G/M: After a quick look round Dubrovnik, which was very beautiful, and where we bought some smoked fat bacon which the kids raved over, we caught the ferry to Corfu.
mileage_note: London to Dubrovnik 1591 miles (Trip total: 1591 miles)

name: Corfu
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We had a week on Allegra, Monique’s step-father's boat, and sailed with him to the Greek mainland and to Paxos, which was a marvellous break from driving and gave us an opportunity to catch our breath.
mileage_note: 707 miles driven through Greece (Trip total: 2298 miles)

name: Istanbul
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We spent a couple of days only. Visited the Topkapi Museum with absolutely fabulous state jewellery, emeralds the size of hen's eggs etc.

name: Bursa
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Staying in town is both tiring and expensive, so we soon headed to Bursa, where a super chap showed us round the mosque. He let us climb the minaret, complete with pigeons, utter darkness, and the odd missing step.

name: Troy
narrative_excerpt: D: We drove on and found a nice view across the sea to Europe, and asked the way to Troy. When we arrived, almost the first thing we saw was an enormous wooden horse; we were able to climb up into it, like the Greeks.

name: Pergamon
narrative_excerpt: G/M: The drive down the coast to Pergamon was very beautiful: enormous trees on the hillsides with glimpses of the sea round most corners. Pergamon was most impressive.

name: Izmir
narrative_excerpt: G/M: On to Izmir where we had 1½ days’ rest. It gets very tiring, touring and visiting and even shopping.

name: Kusadasi
narrative_excerpt: G/M: After Izmir, we went along the coast to Kusadasi, with frequent swims along the way. We found a marvellous place to camp overlooking a beautiful bay, with the town's lights twinkling and a full moon turning night into day.

name: Pamukkale
narrative_excerpt: F: Pammukale is famous for its warm springs and limestone formations. First, the Greeks then the Romans, then the Turks came there.

name: Aspendos
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Onwards towards Antalya on the south coast, for lots more swimming and far too many ruins. We gave Ephesus a miss, apparently a grave mistake, but did get to Aspendos; it is so well-preserved on the outside that we thought we had gone to the wrong place, it looked more like the outside of a medieval Florentine palazzo.

name: Side
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Side was more charming, next to the sea and with a wonderful jumble of fallen statues in the stage area of the theatre; it was particularly impressive as it was not built into the side of a hill but the whole enormous structure was entirely supported by a series of huge arches. It had rather nice-looking public latrines, and some lovely things in the museum, which were in the old baths, it gave D and H “folies de grandeur” and they now want large sunken baths in their ideal house.

name: Alanya
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Side was more charming, next to the sea and with a wonderful jumble of fallen statues in the stage area of the theatre; it was particularly impressive as it was not built into the side of a hill but the whole enormous structure was entirely supported by a series of huge arches. It had rather nice-looking public latrines, and some lovely things in the museum, which were in the old baths, it gave D and H “folies de grandeur” and they now want large sunken baths in their ideal house.

name: Anamur
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We continued along the Turquoise Coast; it was all rather up and down and a long way from the sea, but the scenery was magnificent. We found it rather difficult to find shade for Fred and a nice sandy beach just when we wanted them at midday, and we were very disappointed to find that the prolific bananas were not at all ripe.

name: Narlıkuyu
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We continued along the Turquoise Coast; it was all rather up and down and a long way from the sea, but the scenery was magnificent. We found it rather difficult to find shade for Fred and a nice sandy beach just when we wanted them at midday, and we were very disappointed to find that the prolific bananas were not at all ripe.

name: Cennet ve Cehennem
narrative_excerpt: D: Went to see some caves called “Heaven & Hell”. There was also an “asthma-curing cave”.

name: Nevşehir
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We left the coast at Mersin, after our 2nd puncture. After going through the Gates of Cilicia, we headed for Nevsehir, near which are the vast underground cities of Derinkuyu and Kaymakli.

name: Göreme
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We reluctantly left, and went to Goreme and its famous troglodyte caves. These strange, unearthly conical hills have been produced by natural weathering of the soft rock, and people have taken advantage of this softness to dig churches and monasteries and homes.

name: Ortahisar
narrative_excerpt: D: We left the Mocamp and drove to Ortahisar. In the middle of the small town was a big rock that had been hollowed out into passages and small rooms.

name: Zelve
narrative_excerpt: D: We left the Mocamp and drove to Ortahisar. In the middle of the small town was a big rock that had been hollowed out into passages and small rooms.

name: Kayseri
narrative_excerpt: D: Went to Kayseri, where we met a student who took us round. There was a big high mountain behind, that was capped in snow.

name: Van
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We continued on the long trek east, along miles of roads that were being mended. They seem to let a road degenerate until it is full of potholes and then mend about 60 km at a time, which makes driving along the 60 kms hazardous and frustrating.

name: Urmia (Rezaiyah)
narrative_excerpt: G/M: After taking a very poor road across a secondary entrance into Iran – blowing out a brand-new tyre in the process – we slept the night at the Iranian border. Anyway, we continued on next day to Rezaiyah [currently known as Urmia] to change money, arrange third party insurance, etc.

name: Kermanshah
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We then drove to Kermanshah, where there are some well-preserved 4th century AD bas-reliefs, now set in a large well laid-out (trees and water) picnic area. From Van to Kermanshah is the Kurdish area, and it is very striking to see the Kurdish women striding out unveiled, and with swinging skirts, through towns and country.

name: Sanandaj
narrative_excerpt: D: We stayed the night surrounded by corn stubble fields, some super flocks passed by, but they didn’t trouble us at all. In the morning we drove on to Sanadaj, on the way we stopped and lent some Kurdish people from a Land Rover our jack.

name: Taq-e Bostan
narrative_excerpt: G/M: At Taq-e Boston, we watched with fascination as women walked past us with large, up to 2 ft diameter, metal bowls on their heads, in which was the family washing up. They went to the local pool, with rather grubby-looking water, and scoured all the dishes with sand or earth until they were gleaming.

name: Hamadan
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We slept rather nervously in a new part of the park, but soon discovered to our joy that Iranians are great picnickers, but do not seem to be such persistent starers. Next night, on the road to Hamadan, was finally the last night of the fasting month of Ramadan.

name: Isfahan
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Isfahan was the first really impressive place we saw in Iran. It has many beautiful buildings and lovely old bridges over the river, which runs right through the city. There are gardens and fountains and playgrounds all along the riverbanks.

name: Naqsh-e Rostam
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Some people had told us they found it disappointing, but we found that the many bas-reliefs and carvings were in very good condition and gave very vivid pictures of the people – their dress, hairstyles, make-up even, and of all of the animals and types of chariots, etc.

name: Persepolis
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Some people had told us they found it disappointing, but we found that the many bas-reliefs and carvings were in very good condition and gave very vivid pictures of the people – their dress, hairstyles, make-up even, and of all of the animals and types of chariots, etc.

name: Shiraz
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Our stay in a Persian house was very pleasant. Pariwash had two children, a girl of 13, a boy of 9 and a large house with plenty of room for us. The main problem was food: all absolutely delicious but not always to the children's taste and always mountains of it.

name: Isfahan
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Back to Isfahan, this time to camp alongside one of the river parks. A bit public and a long walk to the nearest loo in the park, but free and rather lovely. We visited more of the beautiful mosques and made several trips to the beautiful bazaar, where we saw craftsmen beating out intricate patterns in copper and brass.

name: Tehran
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Next stop was Tehran. We went via the desert road past Qom. It is a fiercely religious city and infidels are bitterly resented so we contented ourselves with taking a photo of the famous golden mosque with the telephoto lens and leaving it at that.

name: Caspian Sea
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Over high steep mountains, past some little, disused coal-mines and down, down to below sea level and so to the Caspian. The water was reasonably fresh and pleasant to swim in, although along the 30 km of coast we drove there was little actual access to the beach.

name: Golestan National Park
narrative_excerpt: G/M: After quite a long drive we reached the Golestan Wildlife Park, which is supposed to be part of an original forest, untouched by man. It is supposed to have bears, boars, ibex, leopard, etc. but we have only seen ibex way off in the distance.

name: Mashhad
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Unfortunately, Fred chose this moment to break down and so we were taken to a garage where the carburettor, etc. were taken to bits and then reassembled whilst G tried to keep an eye on things and fight his cold. When our guide / con man took us to an old caravanserai and a carpet shop in it our resistance was at a low ebb and we ended up buying three carpets.

name: Herat
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Herat was the most marvellous town – virtually all mud-brick and only the mosque was above two stories high. Cars are almost a rarity and most transport is on foot, a few bicycles and many gaily-decorated horse drawn carts.

name: Lashkar Gah (Bost)
narrative_excerpt: The Arch of Bost is further on: a large arch standing near a hill, for no obvious reason. The hill itself is heavily honeycombed with rooms and shafts and stair-wells.

name: Kandahar
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Kandahar was a momentous place, although dull in itself. Firstly we found the Bakshish Bakery, at which we bought brown bread – real bread you could slice, not flat, chapati-type bread.

name: Kabul
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Finally, we got away and headed for Kabul. We stopped on the way to see the minarets of Ghazni. First, there was a beautiful Timurid house, well restored by Italian architects and turned into a nice little museum.

name: Bamiyan
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Bamiyan is a village in a flattish valley, with steep cliffs on either side. On one side, Buddhist monks carved various Buddhas out of the vertical cliff faces, during the 1st to 5th centuries AD.

name: Shahr-e Zohak (Red City)
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We set off for the north of Afghanistan. We crossed the headwaters of the famous Oxus River, which later on becomes the frontier with Russia, and came out onto the northern plains, which stretch on, over the Oxus and into Russia for hundreds of miles.

name: Ajar Valley
narrative_excerpt: D: We drove through some eerier, but very beautiful gorges until we came to Doab, there, we wanted to turn off to see the beautiful ‘Valley of Kings’ but the way was barred.

name: Mazar-i Sharif
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We set off for the north of Afghanistan. We crossed the headwaters of the famous Oxus River, which later on becomes the frontier with Russia, and came out onto the northern plains, which stretch on, over the Oxus and into Russia for hundreds of miles.

name: Kabul
narrative_excerpt: G/M: To get back to Kabul we took the main, Russian-built road, over the Salang Pass. It is the highest tarmacked pass, says the guide book, in the world, at 14,000 ft.

name: Jalalabad
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Well, we finally dragged both ourselves and Colin from Kabul, after refusing an offer of $500 for transporting 50 kilos of pistachios to Bombay. We went down the Kabul Gorge towards Djellalabad. Dropping 4,000 ft in a few hours driving, the climate seemed unbelievably different – soft and moist with rich, luxuriant vegetation.

name: Hadda
narrative_excerpt: D: In the morning we went to Hadda, with Colin in our car. It was quite interesting, but there were guards watching our every move, we could only walk on the wooden platform floor, etc. they were very fussy. We saw some beautiful buddha faces.

name: Khyber Pass
narrative_excerpt: D: In the morning we went to Hadda, with Colin in our car. It was quite interesting, but there were guards watching our every move, we could only walk on the wooden platform floor, etc. they were very fussy. We saw some beautiful buddha faces.

name: Peshawar
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Colin has re-appeared, to our great delight, especially after we heard his story. He had stopped for a cuppa coming up the Pass and when he got back into his Land Rover, he threw his coat on the seat. When he reached towards the pocket to get a cigarette, he saw a movement and it was a small snake.

name: Darra Adam Khel
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We decided that we just had to visit Darra, a village in the tribal area which makes guns of all types: from copies of the type of gun that was used in the Crimean War to Sten guns, Lee Enfields and all sorts of pistols, revolvers etc. There is a police outpost where law and order officially ends and then you are in tribal areas.

name: Taxila
narrative_excerpt: H: We stayed all morning at Taxila and visited Jandial, which no-one knows what it is really. At Sirkap, we saw some curved walls with some rooms that were the basis of bastions.

name: Rawalpindi
narrative_excerpt: D: At Raul-Pindi we visited the Army Museum, it had some quite interesting things there, from places all over the sub-continent.

name: Islamabad
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We did a quick whizz up to the new capital, Islamabad, but it was very difficult to see much as it is very spread out so we continued on to Lahore, where we were all waiting to come to grips with Kim, as we had been reading his story out loud as bed-time reading.

name: Lahore
narrative_excerpt: G/M: The mosque was enormous, and very beautiful – a wonderful introduction to Mughal architecture. We should have visited the Lahore Fort, which is supposed to be very interesting, but a series of upset tummies and Helena's aversion to anything even remotely spiced rather sapped our energy.

name: Amritsar
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Across the border and into India. It was as usual a long, drawn-out process and we were very sorry for a young Italian couple who had a young child, which was on both the parents’ passports.

name: Nangal
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Nanqal

name: Bhakra Dam
narrative_excerpt: D: In the morning, we set out for Bhakra Dam. We had to stop at the Public Relations office, because a sign said we had to get a permit to see the dam.

name: Chandigarh
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We followed the Grand Trunk Road for a while, which was very impressive as it had huge shade trees and a very wide grass verge on either side for livestock. Soon however, we branched off to the huge Bhakra Dam, a diversion of the Sutlej River for hydro-electricity and irrigation a-la Snowy (in Australia).

name: Pinjore Gardens
narrative_excerpt: D: On the way we stopped at the Pinjor Gardens; they were beautiful. There was a mini-zoo.

name: Shimla
narrative_excerpt: G/M: On the way to Simla we had one of the best unplanned portions of the trip. We had stopped at another Moghul Garden, the Wagh Garden, and found it full of marquees and police in preparation for a visit by the President so we were not very welcome.

name: Delhi
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We arrived in Delhi somewhat earlier than we had originally planned, as were already worrying about shipping the van in Bombay.

name: Agra
narrative_excerpt: F: We packed up and got some gas. Then we went to the poste restante. Denise got a letter. Then we left. On the way to Agra we saw some Sarus cranes; they had lovely red crests.

name: Fatehpur Sikri
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Then we went on to Fatehpur Sikri. It is a city built entirely of red sandstone by Akbar and was only used for about 15 years, so its style is very pure and there is not the usual hodgepodge of any growing city.

name: Bharatpur
narrative_excerpt: D: We drove to Bharatapur Bird Sanctuary. On the way we saw a man on a litter, all covered with blood. When we got to the bird sanctuary, we got a little boat.

name: Sariska
narrative_excerpt: D: We met the Warden of Sariska Game Reserve and arranged to take him back to the game reserve. On the way, we saw a dog eating a carcass, with lots of vultures waiting for it to finish.

name: Jaipur
narrative_excerpt: D: We drove from Sariska to Jaipur. Just before Jaipur, we visited the palace at Amber.

name: Sawai Madhopur
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We had to decide whether to go to Udaipur and Ahmebad or to the reserve of Sawai Madhapur and then Indore. The lure of the tiger proved too strong and we headed east towards Sawai Madhapur on the tracks of the Ashleys, an American family with 4 children of roughly the same age as ours, and Ian and Viv, an English couple in a Landrover called Brenda, whom we had been meeting on and off since Bamiyan.

name: Bombay (Mumbai)
narrative_excerpt: D: We drove on, and at last entered Bombay at 4 pm. As we had been getting closer and closer, it had been getting warmer and warmer. When we actually entered Bombay, it was very hot and sticky.

name: Ajanta Caves
narrative_excerpt: D: We got all ready, but Fred wouldn’t start. In the end, Dad had to clean out all the spark plugs. At last we got going again; the car coughed a lot, but kept going.

name: Bombay (Mumbai)
narrative_excerpt: D: We woke up and drove to Poona, which is a hill resort near Bombay. We drove straight through. The road was very bad and Fred wasn’t working well.

name: Delhi
narrative_excerpt: G/M: We spent a day in Delhi and saw Ranjit and Pravina again. D: When we woke up, there was a beautiful sunrise.

name: Bangkok
narrative_excerpt: G/M: Then we then zoomed off to Bangkok, and this travelling adventure was over. The adventure of settling into a new life in Australia was about to begin.

name: Singapore
narrative_excerpt: D: We arrived 10am Singapore time. We rang up Tan and he send someone to pick us up. Qantas was paying for a Hotel and lunch and dinner for us.

name: Brisbane
narrative_excerpt: D: At last, very very tired, we arrived in Sydney. We collected our luggage and took a bus to the Inter-Australian airport. There, we took an hour flight to Brisbane. From the air, we could see the whole of Sydney, and the Opera House.
